result.summary: Pausanias continues describing the carved Chest of Cypselus, listing the mythological figures on its second side and then the military scenes on its third. He ends by suggesting that the battle scene may show the forces of Melas, ancestor of Cypselus.

scenes.title: Second side of the chest
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the myth scenes and their verse inscriptions: Night with Death and Sleep, Justice, Idas and Marpessa, Alcmena, Menelaus and Helen, Jason and Medea, the Muses, Atlas and Hercules, Ares and Aphrodite, Thetis and Peleus, Perseus.

scenes.title: Third side: the battle scenes
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the military scenes, gives two antiquarian explanations, and proposes that they show the forces of Melas, ancestor of Cypselus, admitted by Aletes into Corinth.

alias_notes.explanation: Enyalius is an old war-god name, here the inscription naming Ares.

notable_quotes.reason: Inscription predicting Atlas will neglect the apples as Hercules approaches.

analysis.text: The chest's crowded mythological scenes are identified by inscriptions, and Pausanias interprets them with literary knowledge.
Pausanias shows antiquarian debate, weighing rival explanations and arguing from Corinthian family history.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias says the chest's inscriptions were in hexameter verse, some in an archaic, boustrophedon style.

language_notes.text: Hexameter is the epic verse line of six metrical feet; the inscriptions on the chest are in verse. 'Ancles' is an old spelling of ankles.
Zeus (Jupiter) took Amphitryon's form while he was away at war, and Hercules was born of this union.
The apples of the Hesperides were guarded golden apples; Atlas will let Hercules's labor proceed by yielding them.
Enyalius is an old war-god's name, here used for Ares, whom the inscription identifies by it.
Antiquarians are scholars of ancient lore; 'consanguinity' means kinship by blood.
'Prima facie' is Latin for 'at first sight'; the sentence says one would not expect Cypselus's ancestor to ignore Corinthian history.

context_notes.text: In Greek myth Night is the mother of Sleep and Death, here shown as twin children in her arms.
Marpessa was courted by both Idas and Apollo; she was given the choice and chose Idas, a mortal.
Peleus had to hold the sea-goddess Thetis through her shape changes, including serpent, to win her; they became parents of Achilles.
Cypselus became tyrant of Corinth in the seventh century BC; the chest was said to be the one in which he was hidden as a baby.

literary_notes.text: The beautiful woman beating the ugly one personifies Justice punishing Injustice, abstract ideas given human form.
The inscription predicts that Atlas will give up the apples, anticipating Hercules's coming success.
Melas's persistence and Aletes's grudging admission sketch both men in a few phrases, and support Pausanias's explanation of the scene.
